population.note: FICTIONAL. ~262M US adults × 14.6% ≈ 38.3M current users. Age bands weighted by adult population share (18–29 ≈20%, 30–49 ≈33%, 50–64 ≈24%, 65+ ≈23%): 1.4+4.6+5.8+2.8 ≈ 14.6. The 65+ rate rose from 9 to 12 because the Medicare Bridge and its Part D successor pay for obesity. Income thirds (19/15/10) average about 14.7. The bottom third rose least: employer retreat hit hourly workforces first, and its gains come mostly from Medicaid-model states and the gray market. Who pays for the 38.3M: ~14.0M diabetes/cardiac/renal-coded coverage (commercial, Medicare, Medicaid); ~6.0M employer weight-management coverage; ~1.6M Medicare obesity demonstration; ~1.2M Medicaid obesity model; ~10.5M brand cash-pay (TrumpRx, LillyDirect, NovoCare); ~5.0M imported generic, compounded or counterfeit product. Total 38.3M. About 6.5M users (2.5% of adults) have neither obesity nor diabetes and take it for 'metabolic health' or longevity. Nearly all of them are inside the cash and gray buckets. Cycling arithmetic: ever 21.0 − current 14.6 = 6.4 pts used and now off. Restarters among current users ≈ 4.4 pts. Prior cyclers now off again ≈ 1.6 pts. Cycled share = (4.4+1.6)/21 ≈ 29%. Total who ever stopped ≈ 6.4+4.4 = 10.8 pts, of whom 4.4 restarted (41%), inside the parent's 36–47% restart range. Ever-use grows slower than churn alone would predict because one-year persistence improved from ~35% to ~40% on cheaper orals, and because more starts are restarts. Pediatric: ~73M under-18s × 0.9% ≈ 650k, mostly ages 12–17. Ages 6–11 are ~90k after the 2027 label extension, skewed to upper-income and specialist-access families. Never-able-to-afford: of ~95M adults with obesity, roughly 60% have never used, concentrated in the bottom third and in non-expansion Medicaid states.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot ran Jul 2026–Dec 2027 and passed in Jan 2028 into the Part D obesity demonstration CMS had already scheduled. Terms are unchanged: Medicare pays ~$245/month and the beneficiary copay is ~$50. No new legislation. About 1.6M beneficiaries use it for obesity: 1.6M × $245 × 12 ≈ $4.7B/yr gross federal, consistent with CBO's ≥$35B 2026–2034 ramp. Medicaid: the same-rate model is opt-in. ~22 states participate, ~1.2M enrollees: 1.2M × $245 × 12 ≈ $3.5B/yr gross, federal and state combined. Non-participating states cover diabetes codes only.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide is sold in ~160 countries. India: 60+ brands at ~$6–40/month. Canada: ~CAD 70–110/month from six generic makers. Brazil and China (patent lapsed 2026) are major producers; Chinese API underpins most of the gray supply. Tirzepatide is still brand-only everywhere except via counterfeit.
access.note: Managed decline: TrumpRx and manufacturer-direct injectables stepped from ~$350 to $245 (2027) and to $199 for starting doses (2028). Top-dose Zepbound and Wegovy cash tops out around $299. Foundayo and oral Wegovy start at $149. List prices are unchanged (Wegovy $1,349) and almost nobody pays them. Employer weight-management coverage fell 60% → 44% (Business Group on Health, Jan 2028). Among employers that still cover it, GLP-1s are ~14% of pharmacy claims, eligibility is BMI ≥35 or comorbidity, and many require lifestyle-programme enrolment. Where coverage survives, it is mostly diabetes, cardiac (SELECT label), sleep-apnea, MASH and CKD codes. Patients and physicians report 'code-shopping' for qualifying diagnoses. The gray market grew from ~2M to ~5M users (~13% of users) as the 503B exclusion took effect and compounders were squeezed. It routes through Canadian online pharmacies, Indian mail-order, 'research peptide' sites and counterfeit pens sold through social commerce. Orals are ~35% of new starts; weekly injectables still lead the installed base.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic; pediatric label extended to 6+ in 2027)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Mar 2027)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028, dysesthesia warning)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in obesity (tirzepatide, 2027)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' and longevity use by people without obesity or diabetes, ~2.5% of US adults, mostly low-dose orals via telehealth longevity clinics and cash channels
alcohol reduction: semaglutide phase 3 in AUD under way, no approval; widely prescribed off-label by addiction medicine
'muscle-sparing stacks': GLP-1 plus testosterone, SARMs (enobosarm-type, gray-sourced) or compounded peptides, sold by men's-health telehealth
pediatric off-label below age 6 under specialist care (rare)
drugs.pipeline_note: CagriSema was under review at the start of the window and was approved Mar 2027. Novo markets it on tolerability, not efficacy, after REDEFINE-4. Retatrutide's NDA was filed Feb 2027 and approved Apr 2028, 14 months after filing. It carries a dysesthesia warning and launched at a $299 cash cap; it holds the best efficacy at 28%. The drawn muscle-preserving combination cannot be on the US market under phase rules, so it is realised as follows. Lilly's bimagrumab + tirzepatide phase 2b (Feb 2027) reported ~90% of weight lost as fat, and phase 3 began mid-2027; earliest US filing is ~2029 and launch ~2030. Novo's amycretin is still in phase 3. Veru's enobosarm + semaglutide is in phase 3. Even so, the 'skinny-frail problem' is widely sold as solved: through investor coverage of the phase 2b data, through CagriSema and retatrutide marketing language about 'higher-quality weight loss', and through off-label telehealth stacks. Survodutide filed 2028. MariTide (monthly) is in phase 3, not on market. Global incretin market ~$118B in 2028; volume is up sharply but net price is down.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of discontinuation. Higher in gray-market users because of dose confusion (mg vs 'units') with reconstituted vials.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis' (Jan 2025).

safety_ledger.effect: Gastroparesis, ileus and bowel obstruction, incl. claims of persistence after discontinuation
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Delayed gastric emptying is pharmacological and established. Ileus is labelled. Whether severe gastroparesis persists after stopping is contested: case series exist, and cohort data are confounded by diabetes. MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) passed 30,000 filed cases in 2028 after a 2027 ruling let gastroparesis claims proceed where a gastric-emptying study documents the injury. First bellwether set for early 2029.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added ileus/obstruction language to remaining labels in 2027; no new restriction. Manufacturers have booked litigation reserves; no settlement.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss; higher absolute numbers with retatrutide-scale loss.

Long-term RCTs still do not confirm causation; absolute risk low. Pancreatitis is now the second-largest injury category in MDL 3094. Plaintiffs' pancreatic-cancer claims were mostly dismissed for lack of general causation in 2028.

~25–40% of weight lost is lean mass, larger at retatrutide-scale loss; concern centres on adults 65+ now entering via Medicare. The bone-density signal persists. Public belief that the problem is 'solved' runs ahead of the evidence: no muscle-preserving agent is approved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. Industry response is combination drugs in phase 3 and 'protein + strength' companion programmes.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict. Added to MDL 3094 as a minor claim category.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label for semaglutide; no US class label.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Anecdote only; still not quantified. Press attention faded after 2026, and a 2027 pooled analysis of trial mood questionnaires found no difference, though the instruments were not built to detect it. The litigation bar ignores it because it is not a provable injury. Same mechanism as the alcohol-use benefit.
Trial data still show most weight regained within a year. Real-world data are still mixed. Cyclers report regain concentrated as fat, not muscle.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; underpins chronic-therapy framing and payer reluctance.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: More case reports in low-intake and longevity users, and in children; no systematic estimate.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; professional societies recommend dietitian review.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in children (now from age 6) who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist for semaglutide. There are still no data for growth or puberty beyond about two years in the 6–11 trial, and none on cycling, which now covers ~29% of ever-users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The pediatric approval carries a postmarketing growth-and-development registry requirement.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded, imported and counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination, mislabelled or substituted contents)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FDA adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~6,000. In 2027 a CDC cluster investigation found 61 hospitalisations and 2 deaths from bacterially contaminated vials sold online. Poison-control calls for GLP-1 overdose roughly tripled from 2025. Seized counterfeit pens included some containing insulin.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Routine enforcement only: warning letters, import alerts on named sites, the finalised 503B exclusion. No new statute or programme.

safety_ledger.effect: 'Muscle-sparing stack' harms (SARMs, testosterone, unapproved peptides taken alongside GLP-1s)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Case reports of liver injury, polycythaemia and lipid derangement in men's-health telehealth users; no estimate.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning letters to a handful of telehealth firms.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~28% of US households. Salty-snack and confectionery volumes are down ~4–6% from 2025, and per-trip basket calories are measurably lower. Revenue is defended by price-pack architecture: smaller packs at higher unit prices. High-protein, fibre and 'portion' SKUs are now standard, not niche. Under the aesthetic inversion, a counter-segment of 'real food, full plate' premium brands is gaining with affluent non-users. Several mid-cap snack makers merged or sold divisions.

alcohol.state: US spirits volume is down a further ~5% in the window. Heavy-drinker attrition is the main driver: off-label addiction-medicine prescribing plus incidental on-drug reduction. Brown-Forman and Diageo have cut US headcount. Bars lean on premium 'one good drink' pricing; no-alcohol lines are growing but do not replace lost revenue.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. Cheap thinness has given visible appetite a status value: in Austin, Brooklyn and LA, high-end restaurants market tasting menus 'for appetites' and family-style feasts. Fast-casual chains push protein bowls and smaller sizes, and the middle of casual dining keeps losing check size.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking: store closures, and one chain in restructuring. Mainstream apparel's re-sizing wave is over. Growth is in athletic and 'built' fits for men and women, cut for shoulders and glutes rather than slimness.

fitness.state: Strength gyms and coached lifting are the fastest-growing segment, driven by both muscle-preservation messaging to users and a 'natty' status culture among non-users. GLP-1 companion programmes are a standard employer-wellness product. Budget cardio chains are flat.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is down to 44%, with tighter eligibility. Coverage has concentrated on diabetes, cardiac, sleep-apnea and renal codes, which drives diagnosis-code gaming and prior-authorisation disputes. Some carriers price riders for weight management as optional, employee-paid add-ons.

pharma.state: Lilly and Novo still dominate. Lilly leads on retatrutide and Foundayo; Novo is weakened, with CagriSema a tolerability play. Volumes are up sharply, net price is down ~30% from 2026, and ex-US revenue is eroding to generics. Litigation reserves are a visible line item. A field of ~800 GLP-1R molecules is pushing toward the 2031–32 exclusivity cliff.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness has stopped signalling discipline or money. With $149 pills and $40 Canadian generics, a slim body reads as 'on something', and the default assumption is cheap product. The scarce signals are muscle mass, a visible appetite and the claim to be 'natty': unmedicated, borrowed from bodybuilding slang. 'Unmedicated vitality' is a brand category in wellness marketing, and the phrase is half-ironic.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The class gradient has partly inverted. Professional women aged 25–40 in Brooklyn and Austin increasingly treat being on a GLP-1 as faintly déclassé, or hide it. They invest instead in coached strength training, protein-heavy diets and visible eating, all of which cost time and money. At the same time, the bottom income third still has the least access to brand product and the most exposure to counterfeits. Many affluent people are themselves quiet low-dose 'metabolic health' users, so the natty ideal is partly performance.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Two dining cultures sit side by side: the small plate and protein shake of the medicated majority, and the conspicuous feast of the status minority. 'Hungry' has become a compliment in some circles. Family meals in GLP-1 households, now including some with medicated children, run on smaller portions and fewer snacks.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles in big cities carry 'natty' or 'on GLP-1' as informal tags. Anecdotes of muted desire on-drug persist but are rarely named. Muscle has replaced slimness as the most-mentioned physical attraction in app survey data.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is now a choice in both directions: something medicated away, or something displayed. For children aged 6–11 it is, for the first time, something a pediatrician may prescribe against.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Anecdote only. The 2026 'Ozempic personality' coverage did not develop into data. A 2027 pooled analysis of trial mood questionnaires found nothing, though the instruments were not designed to find it. Litigation, which is now the main engine of drug-harm attention, ignores it. Whatever prevalence exists is unmeasured, and it is spread across 38M users and ~6.5M non-obese longevity users who were never screened for mood at baseline.
interior_life.framing: Not named as a drug effect. Quieted wanting, where it happens, is read as calm, maturity, 'finally not being hungry', or simply the decade. In addiction medicine the same mechanism is called treatment. Nobody connects the two in public.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Nothing measurable has been reported. Managers anecdotally note fewer after-work drinks and earlier departures from team events. Some users describe steadier focus, a few describe 'not caring about the promotion'. Nobody attributes either to the drug.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Unattributed. Bar trivia, late comedy shows and heavy-pour wine events report thinner crowds, usually blamed on alcohol trends. Intense-flavour foods and extreme-sour candy keep growing. Adult recreational leagues and lifting gyms grow, partly through the natty culture.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Unattributed. Couples therapists hear 'we just don't want much' without a cause named. Individual reports of lower desire circulate in forums and are treated as personal.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: None observable. No constituency forms around an effect nobody has named.

state.regulatory_posture: No new state action. The FDA continues its existing posture: speedy approvals (CagriSema, retatrutide, the pediatric label) and routine enforcement against compounders and import sites, including the 503B exclusion finalised from the 2026 proposal. There is no new statute, programme or emergency response to the counterfeit surge. Personal-importation enforcement discretion is unchanged.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The negotiated $245/$50 Medicare rate continues through the already-scheduled Part D demonstration. Medicaid participation is state opt-in (~22 states). The TrumpRx cash channel continues at lower prices under pre-existing deals.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged in kind: BMI and comorbidity criteria and prior authorisation. Some employers that still cover it require enrolment in a lifestyle programme. No adherence monitoring by the state.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US price gap is starker: brand ~$149–299 vs Indian generic ~$6–40 and Canadian ~CAD 70–110. Health Canada and provincial pharmacy regulators restricted cross-border bulk sales in 2027 after shortage complaints, which pushed US gray buyers toward Indian and Chinese-API sources with weaker quality control. Brand exclusivity in the US still runs to ~2031–32.

events.event: Lilly's bimagrumab-plus-tirzepatide phase 2b shows ~90% of weight lost as fat; phase 3 begins. 'The skinny-frail problem is solved' headlines run, and men's-health telehealth firms launch off-label 'muscle-sparing stacks' within weeks
FDA approves Wegovy for children aged 6–11 with obesity on an sNDA, with a required growth-and-development registry; pediatric endocrinology waitlists lengthen in affluent metros

CDC links 61 hospitalisations and 2 deaths in nine states to bacterially contaminated semaglutide vials sold through 'research peptide' websites; poison-control GLP-1 calls are running about three times 2025 levels

Business Group on Health: only 44% of large employers now cover GLP-1s for weight management, down from 60%. Medicare's Bridge pilot rolls into the pre-scheduled Part D demonstration at the same $245/$50 terms, with no new legislation

GLP-1 multidistrict litigation in Philadelphia passes 30,000 filed cases, led by gastroparesis, ileus and pancreatitis claims; Novo and Lilly disclose litigation reserves; first bellwether set for 2029

Gallup: 14.6% of US adults are on an incretin drug, and roughly one in six users has neither obesity nor diabetes. The same survey finds 'natural' or 'unmedicated' bodies rated most desirable by adults under 40

open_tensions: A two-tier system has hardened: diagnosis-coded and Medicare patients get brand product, and the uncovered middle pays $149–299 cash or drifts to imports. The counterfeit harms fall on the people coverage abandoned, and no institution has taken ownership of the problem.

Mass-tort litigation over gastroparesis and pancreatitis heads to bellwether trials in 2029; a plaintiff verdict could reshape labels, prescribing to non-obese longevity users, and pediatric enthusiasm at once.
The 'skinny-frail' problem is believed solved two years before any muscle-preserving drug can launch, while retatrutide-scale weight loss reaches Medicare-age bodies now.

Children from age 6 are starting drugs they may take for decades, inside a culture that has begun to despise the thinness the drugs produce, with no data on cycling, growth or what quieted wanting does to a developing mind.

There is still no FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US; brand exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32

Foundayo (orforglipron) and the Wegovy pill are still sold at $149 for initial doses through cash channels

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: The $149 Body, the $40 Fake, and the New Rich Who Want You to Watch Them Eat
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, and the striking thing is how little the country looks different from the street. The difference is in how things are paid for and who receives them. The drugs are cheaper than they were and still not cheap. A starting dose of Foundayo or the Wegovy pill costs $149 a month through the government's cash channel. Injectables step down to $199 and top out near $299, and retatrutide has entered at the top of that band, promising more than a quarter of body weight. Insurance, meanwhile, has largely walked away from obesity as obesity. Fewer than half of large employers still cover the drugs for weight. What survives is coverage for diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea and failing kidneys, so doctors and patients have learned which codes open doors. Medicare's pilot ended on schedule and folded into the demonstration that was already planned, at the same $245 and the same $50 copay. Washington did nothing new and nobody expected it to.

Between the covered and the comfortable sits the gray market, now about five million people. Some order from Canadian pharmacies, though Ottawa has tightened that tap. Some buy Indian generics for the price of a lunch. Some buy pens from strangers on social commerce that turn out to contain something else. A batch of contaminated vials put sixty-one people in hospital in 2027 and killed two. Poison-control lines field calls from people who confused milligrams with units. The harm is real, local and spread thin, which is why it has not yet become anybody's job.

The lawyers have found the injury they can prove. More than thirty thousand cases sit in a Philadelphia courtroom, built on gastric-emptying studies, bowel obstructions and pancreatitis admissions, and the companies now book reserves against them. Nothing in that litigation concerns what users describe in quieter terms: wanting less, of everything. That complaint had a moment in 2026 and then dissolved into ordinary life. People who feel flatter call it calm, or age, or finally being free of food. Addiction doctors prescribe the same effect off-label for heavy drinkers and call it treatment.

The drug has also moved beyond the sick. About one user in six has neither obesity nor diabetes. They are longevity clients, metabolic optimisers, people who saw what a low-dose pill did for a colleague. And since 2027 pediatricians can prescribe semaglutide to six-year-olds, which they do mostly in the zip codes where families can find a pediatric endocrinologist.

The culture has answered cheap thinness the way it answers anything cheap: by moving the prize. In Austin and Brooklyn and the expensive parts of Los Angeles, the coveted body is muscled and visibly fed. Status belongs to the person who lifts with a coach four mornings a week and orders the whole fish, and the word for it is natty. Tasting menus are sold 'for appetites'. Plus-size retailers keep closing stores while lifting gyms open them. Snack companies sell smaller bags at higher unit prices and survive. Distillers do not have an equivalent move and are laying people off.

The pharmaceutical industry has meanwhile sold the country a solution it does not yet have. A muscle-sparing combination posted good phase 2 data and began phase 3. Within weeks the phrase 'skinny-frail is solved' was everywhere, and telehealth companies were shipping testosterone and gray-market SARMs alongside semaglutide. The combination itself cannot reach pharmacies before about 2030. Medicare-age patients are losing retatrutide-scale weight now.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dana Ruiz, forty-one, takes her Foundayo at 6:10 with water, standing at the counter so she doesn't forget. Ninety-nine days in. The TrumpRx charge, $149, posts while she makes her son's lunch. The dental group dropped weight coverage last January. Her sister Marisol says the Canadian stuff is the same molecule. Dana has read about the vials in Houston and keeps paying.

Mateo is nine and asks why her breakfast is just yogurt. She says she isn't hungry, which is true and also the whole point.

At work, between cleanings, the front-desk girl shows everyone a video of her boyfriend deadlifting. "He's natty," she says, as if that settles something. Dana's patient at eleven is a retired welder on Medicare who pays fifty dollars for his shots and has lost so much his dentures slip. She makes a note for the dentist.

At lunch the hygienists split one order of tacos four ways. Nobody finishes.

The pediatrician's office calls back about Mateo's BMI. They can get him in with the specialist in San Antonio in March, and insurance may cover it under the new label if his A1c qualifies. Dana says she'll think about it.

At six she meets an old friend at a place on South Congress where the menu says FEED ME. The friend has new shoulders and orders the whole fish and eats it slowly, and Dana watches.

On the drive home Dana realises she hasn't wanted the radio on in weeks. She turns it on, listens to a song she used to love, and turns it off again. Nothing feels wrong to her.
